Ša nagba imuru

The Epic of Gilgamesh

The twelve-tablet epic of the king of Uruk — the cedar forest, the Bull of Heaven, the flood, and the search for everlasting life. The world’s first great literary work.

Anonymous (Akkadian) c. 18th–7th century BC (standard version)
12 Sections
6 Temples named

English (Thompson, 1928) — R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928). License: Public domain. Source.

Forth went the hunter, took with him a courtesan-girl, a hetaera, (So) did they start on their travels, went forth on their journey (together), (Aye), at the term of three days arrived at the pleasaunce appointed. (O but) a monster (all) savage from out of the depths of the desert!

"'Tis he, O girl! O, discover thy beauty, thy comeliness shew (him),

Ravish the soul of him--(certes), as soon as his eye on thee falleth,

So that he clasp thee, and (then) with the wiles of a woman shalt ply him;

(Wherefore) his animals, bred in his desert, will (straightway) deny him,

(Since) to his breast he hath held thee. "

The girl, displaying her bosom, Shew'd him her comeliness, (yea) so that he of her beauty possess'd him,

Bashful she was not, (but) ravish'd the soul of him, loosing her mantle,

So that he clasp'd her, (and then) with the wiles of a woman she plied him,

Holding her unto his breast.

1I.e., a seal-cylinder or amulet of chalcedony. 2The Annual festival of the Wailing for Tammuz. Tammuz, the husband of Ishtar, representing vegetation, dies each year in the Autumn, and his faithful spouse goes down to the Underworld to bring him back with the return of Spring. The Roller, a brightly coloured bird which lives in the palm groves of Southern Babylonia, uttering a hoarse cry which may be identified with kappi.
